newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST -Hefty UK Feb PSBR not to threaten target.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -Hefty UK Feb PSBR not to threaten target.

text.p: Britain's public sector debt is forecast to amount to nearly four billion stg in February, nearly one billion more than in the same month last year, economists said on Monday.
But that should not stop the public sector borrowing requirement sliding comfortably under the government's 26.4 billion stg target for the whole financial year ending in March.
A Reuter poll of economists produced a consensus forecast for a 3.7 billion stg government overspend last month. In February 1996, it was only 2.95 billion stg.

But following a massive 5.8 billion stg debt repayment in January, as corporate tax and value added tax receipts flooded into the government's coffers, the 1996/97 target looks distinctly unchallenging.

"Altogether, these figures suggest that the government's forecast for 1996/97 will be undershot, with the outcome likely to fall between 23 and 24 billion pounds," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc.
Shaw said February usually suffers from an absence of corporation tax -- the most buoyant of the inflows. He forecast a government revenue shortfall of 3.5 billion stg.
Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, expected a much larger, 5.0 billion stg deficit in February.

Nonetheless, he agreed that the government's target for the year would not be missed. "We expect government spending to be reined in as the end of the fiscal year approaches and remain comfortable with our forecast of a full year deficit of 25.5 billion," he said.
The cumulative public sector debt for the year so far is 10.34 billion stg, much smaller than the 19.33 billion stg debt amassed over the same period last year.
March is often afflicted by a heavy government overspend as departments shell out whatever they have left in their budgets. But it would have to be huge to threaten the government's target.
As for February, Barr said VAT receipts would suffer after January's bonanza, adding that there were no privatisation proceeds to massage the figures last month.
